features.title: Preview session and runtime lifecycle
features.summary: The Preview session and runtime generation lifecycle: session and generation identity and history, reload, restart and reconnect boundaries, and automatic and explicit recovery of a failed generation.

rules.statement: A Preview session spans iframe reloads, runtime restarts, transport reconnects, View and Variant navigation and generation changes; only a new Preview instance starts a new session.
The Workbench never activates a Preview session whose ID matches one retired earlier in the same Workbench process; it discards that ID and generates another before the session begins.
After a full Workbench restart, an open Workbench page starts a new Preview session, with a fresh generation and newly acquired geometry, before any geometry traffic resumes.
A runtime generation that becomes protocol-invalid ends only that generation, never the enclosing Preview session.
After a generation becomes protocol-invalid, the runtime may start one fresh generation automatically in the same Preview session, with its own declaration and acknowledgement.
If the automatic recovery generation also becomes protocol-invalid during its handshake, no further generation starts until the Workbench authorizes an explicit retry.
The automatic recovery allowance renews only when a fresh generation completes its handshake; creating a generation, declaring capabilities, reconnecting or waiting never renews it.
While recovery is exhausted and no retry is authorized, the Workbench never acknowledges a new generation or accepts its traffic.
The Workbench retires the ID of a generation it refused while recovery was exhausted, without ending the Preview session.
While Preview capability is unavailable, the Workbench sends and accepts no geometry traffic.
While Preview capability is unavailable, the Workbench keeps the structural Widget selection.
While Preview capability is unavailable, the Workbench shows the Widget highlight as unavailable.
One explicit retry authorizes exactly one fresh-generation attempt.
When the generation an explicit retry started fails, Preview returns to capability-unavailable.
When the generation an explicit retry started fails, the automatic recovery allowance stays spent.
A retry authorization is spent when its fresh generation enters bootstrap, whatever the outcome of that generation's handshake.
A pending retry authorization lasts until it is spent, revoked or its Preview session ends; nothing else, not even elapsed time, expires it.
A retry trigger while an authorization is pending joins that authorization, so retry attempts never accumulate.
The Workbench may revoke a pending retry authorization until its generation enters bootstrap.
Revoking a retry authorization and admitting its generation are serialized, and whichever commits first wins.
A retry trigger while an authorized generation is still in its handshake creates no authorization and never replaces or cancels that generation.
Iframe reloads, runtime restarts, reconnects and View or Variant navigation never clear exhausted recovery or authorize a new generation.
A new Preview session starts with an unspent automatic recovery allowance, no unavailable state and no retry authorization.

After a generation change the Workbench hides every highlight of the old generation and draws it again only from a complete geometry set acquired under the new generation, never showing old contours meanwhile.

## Notes

- Added beyond the plan's Feature list: Discussion #1 comments 120-148 (session, generation and capability lifecycle) had no Feature home. Per the owner's Q1 ruling the wire-level detail will be Clauses of the Preview protocol Contract (message types and invariants only).
- The wire side of the lifecycle is owned by the Preview protocol Contract: identities by {{C.preview-protocol.session-id}} and {{C.preview-protocol.generation-id}}, retirement and reuse by {{C.preview-protocol.generation-reuse}}, the gates and stale traffic by {{C.preview-protocol.gates}}, the handshake by {{C.preview-protocol.handshake-gate}}, {{C.preview-protocol.declaration-pinning}} and {{C.preview-protocol.retransmission}}, and reload, restart and reconnect by {{C.preview-protocol.generation-boundaries}} and {{C.preview-protocol.generation-scope}}.

features.title: Widget navigation and highlight
features.summary: Navigating to a Widget from Checks: structural selection, the Workbench-drawn highlight and how it tracks, hides and is restored, translucent-coverage notices, comment-mode deferral, and fallbacks for missing Views and Widgets.

rules.statement: Navigating to a Widget from Checks opens its View and selects the Widget by its stable identity in the View structure, whether or not the Preview currently shows it.
Navigation never switches the Variant, forces a hidden Widget visible, changes Widget State or rebuilds the runtime to show its target.
When the target is rendered and visible but scrolled out of the Preview viewport, the Preview scrolls its own content to it before the Workbench highlights it.
When the target is not rendered or has no visible part, the Workbench keeps it selected, draws no highlight and shows that it is not visible in the current Preview.

When the target's visibility or contour precision cannot be established, the Workbench keeps it selected, draws no highlight and says that precise highlighting is unavailable, distinctly from a target that is not visible.
A visible target's highlight follows the Widget's current geometry as it moves, resizes or reflows, updated by change events at most once per animation frame, never frozen or polled.
When the highlight's geometry becomes unavailable, stale or invalid, the Workbench hides the highlight at once and redraws it only from fresh, valid geometry for the current target and context.
The highlight covers only the reported visible part of the Widget, never a part clipped by the viewport or an ancestor or covered by an opaque element.
When the visible part splits into disconnected regions, the Workbench outlines every reported region, still as one selected Widget and one navigation.
The highlight strokes only the outer perimeter of each visible region, never fills it and draws no inner ring around a hidden area that the region encloses.
Fragmented or partly covered visibility never adds Checks findings, changes affected View or Widget counts or creates extra selections.
When the target is still discernible under a translucent covering element, the Workbench shows one shared notice beside the highlight and a matching current-state marker on the Widget's Checks entry.

The translucent notice and its Checks marker describe only the current Preview state, change or disappear with the target, context or coverage, and are hidden while comment mode suspends the highlight.
Highlight stroke width is set in final Workbench pixels, so zooming or scaling the Preview never thickens or thins it.
The Preview reports geometry and visibility only; highlight color, dash, opacity and glow come from Workbench design tokens.
Entering comment mode hides the Checks highlight and stops tracking it, keeping the Widget selected and its target saved; comment targeting geometry keeps working.
On leaving comment mode the Workbench restores the saved highlight only after revalidating its target and receiving fresh geometry, never reusing coordinates from before comment mode.
A Checks navigation requested during comment mode is queued instead of run, and a later request replaces the queued one.
On leaving comment mode, the queued navigation runs and takes precedence over restoring the earlier highlight.
When a Checks navigation, immediate or queued, targets a Widget that no longer exists in a surviving View, the Workbench opens that View, selects no other Widget and draws no highlight.
A missing target Widget is reported by a persistent, non-modal inline notice in the navigation context until that context is replaced or left.

When a Checks navigation targets a View that no longer exists, the Workbench stays on the current screen, keeps the selection, hides the previous Checks highlight and shows a non-blocking notice that navigation did not happen.
A failed navigation is cleared: it never restores an earlier or comment-suspended highlight and never replays an older request.

## Notes

- The wire side is owned by the Preview protocol Contract: messages by {{C.preview-protocol.geometry-messages}}, the coordinate space by {{C.preview-protocol.coordinates}}, stream identity, lifecycle, reporting and gates by {{C.preview-protocol.stream-identity}}, {{C.preview-protocol.stream-lifecycle}}, {{C.preview-protocol.stream-reports}} and {{C.preview-protocol.stream-gates}}, and revisions by {{C.preview-protocol.geometry-revision}}. That the Workbench, not the iframe, draws the highlight is owned by {{R.preview.isolation.review-chrome}}; what clipping, occlusion and compositing leave visible is owned by {{R.preview.geometry.true-shape}}, {{R.preview.geometry.opaque-proof}}, {{R.preview.geometry.translucent-kept}} and {{R.preview.geometry.unprovable}}, and the hole tracing of Discussion #1 c98 is superseded by #1 c100 ({{R.preview.geometry.outer-contour}}, {{R.preview.navigation.outline-only}}). When the highlight is precise enough to draw is owned by {{R.preview.geometry.precision-gate}} and {{C.preview-protocol.display-tolerance}}.
- Owner ruling 2026-10-07 (batch 6b confirmation): Discussion #1 c80 and c81 stay normative for {{R.preview.navigation.scroll-offscreen}}, with its implementation gap. #2 c35 adds no navigation-control message and #2 c36 (decision 7, alternative 10) speaks only of pin edge indicators, so neither amends them; the reveal mechanism (a new runtime command, or a Checks acquisition that also reveals) needs its own architecture decision, tracked in the issue that the gap names.
- Not imported: the default stroke of 2 Workbench CSS pixels (#2 c29 d1) and the indicator's top-right placement and collision handling (#2 c29 d4) are Workbench presentation tokens; how Checks groups and orders findings is owned by the Checks Feature.

features.title: Click-to-comment targeting
features.summary: Targeting interactions in the Preview: the Select and Comment modes, hit testing, hover candidates and commits, Escape, focus and teardown, pins in comment mode, and suppressing Widget Events while targeting.

rules.statement: The Select tool holds an inspection interaction, the Comment tool a comment-range interaction, and the Interact tool none.
Without an active interaction the Preview reports no hover candidate or commit, so clicks under the Interact tool never cross the boundary.
During targeting the Workbench never covers the Preview with a capture layer, forwards synthetic pointer events into it or infers the target from cached geometry.
A hover candidate is drawn as a transient, non-interactive outline from current stream geometry only, and becomes the structural selection only when committed.
Touch input has no hover candidate, and a tap commits the target.
Escape pressed inside the Preview during comment mode is only an intent: the Workbench performs the mode exit, clears its overlays and runs any queued navigation.
Moving focus from the Preview to Workbench UI clears the hover candidate but does not exit the targeting mode.
A generation change during targeting discards that generation's uncommitted targeting state; the mode may stay, accepting input again only after the new generation completes its handshake.
While any targeting interaction is active, whatever its purpose, no Widget Event advances the Prototype player, and none from that time is replayed afterwards.
In comment mode, clicking a pin, pin cluster or edge indicator opens its thread instead of starting a new comment, while pointer input elsewhere still reaches the Preview.
Under the Select tool a click commits the Widget as the selection and still reaches the Widget's own handlers in the Preview.

features.title: Visible Widget geometry
features.summary: Widget geometry in the Workbench and the Preview: per-Widget geometry streams and the tracked-Widget cap, the mapping from the Preview content box to the overlay, pin tracking and visibility, visible-region contours and their occlusion classification, and contour precision, refinement and caching.

rules.statement: The Workbench maps reported geometry into its overlay from the browser's actual rendering of the Preview content box, treating configured zoom or scale values as inputs, never as the mapping itself.

Moving, scaling, zooming or transforming the Preview from outside, scrolling the Workbench or changing the iframe border never requests new geometry or advances a revision; the Workbench reprojects the latest accepted geometry while it can still measure the mapping.

When the Preview content viewport changes size, the Workbench hides every highlight and pin at once and reopens every geometry stream under a fresh identity, so geometry measured before the resize never shows.

When the Workbench cannot reliably measure how the Preview is rendered, it draws no highlight, outline or pin, substitutes no bounding box, configured value or last-known mapping, and keeps the structural selection.

Without a browser API that reports the content-box quad, the Workbench accepts its box measurement only after proving every transform up the flat tree is a translation with uniform positive scale; any failed proof, including an SVG ancestor, means unmeasurable.
The Preview measures a Widget's box only under the same transform proof, and a Widget outside it reports no visible region, so rotated or skewed Widgets get no highlight or pin.

The Workbench tracks outer-mapping changes by events and measures the rendered mapping at most once per animation frame per Preview, shared by every overlay, with no frame loop while no overlay is shown.
While pins are the only overlay, the Workbench measures only after a change signal or during an animation, so shown pins with nothing changing cost no frame callbacks and no messages.
The Workbench keeps at most one geometry stream per Widget and shares its reports with every consumer of that Widget: the highlight, the hover outline, pins and a pending composer.

When demand exceeds the stream cap, streams go first to the open or selected thread, the pending composer and the hover candidate, then the selection highlight, then pinned Widgets by thread status, newest activity and Widget identity.
Without concurrent geometry streams, a hover candidate takes the only stream, and the selection outline stays hidden while a candidate exists.
A thread whose Widget gets no stream draws no pin, never a last-known one, and its Comments entry says that it is not shown on the canvas and suggests narrowing the pin filter.
Pins stay tracked and visible during comment-range targeting, including during a gesture; only the Checks highlight is suspended.
A pin is drawn only from its Widget's current accepted report, and only when its point lies inside a reported visible region, farther from that region's edge than the region's reported error bound.
Proven translucent coverage never hides a pin.
The Workbench draws pins only while the Preview's outer mapping is affine, so a non-affine mapping hides every pin even when a precise highlight can still be proven.
Pins never request contour precision work.

A pinned Widget wholly outside the Preview viewport, or mapped outside the visible canvas stage, gets an edge indicator from its current rectangle; clicking it opens the thread and never scrolls the Preview.
Pins close together on screen merge into a count cluster recomputed from current positions, and a cluster never keeps a member whose geometry is not current.
The Preview reports each disconnected, reliably visible piece of a Widget as one closed outer contour, and never computes or reports contours of interior holes.
The Preview converts quadratic curves and circular or elliptical arcs into cubic segments before reporting them, and reports no contour whose conversion error it cannot bound.
The Preview derives every clipped or occluded outline from the actual shape of the clip or occluder, never from a bounding box or a heuristic approximation.
A covering element cuts the Widget's visible region only where the Preview proves that the Widget contributes nothing to the covered pixels; near-opaque thresholds and style heuristics never suffice.

Coverage that the Preview proves translucent, leaving the Widget visibly discernible, keeps the covered area in the visible region and marks it as translucently covered; no alpha or contrast threshold decides it.
Mixed opaque and translucent coverage is classified area by area from each area's own proven status, never by one overlap rule for the whole Widget.

When compositing, masks, filters, an occluder transform outside the measurable subset or any other paint over the Widget leave its contribution or visible perimeter unproven, the Preview invents no classification or contour and reports no precise visible region.
The Preview reports when it cannot establish a Widget's visible region or contour precision, distinctly from reporting that no part of the Widget is visible.
Precise clipping supports at least opaque rectangles and rounded boxes, clip-path basic shapes and polygons, and geometric SVG clip paths, whenever the Preview can derive their actual shape.

The Workbench draws a Widget's precise highlight only while every one of its contours meets the display tolerance under the current outer mapping, and otherwise hides the whole highlight, never only the failing regions.

When an outer change makes a cached contour miss the display tolerance, the Workbench requests finer contours for the unchanged geometry instead of remeasuring the Widget, and restores the highlight only from a result that meets it.
The Workbench refines only the regions that miss the display tolerance, and requests a complete regeneration instead when the cached regions cannot be matched by identity in the current geometry.
The Workbench keeps one complete contour cache per Widget geometry revision and replaces it only with a complete set that is no less precise overall, never merely because a response is newer.
Merging a partial result keeps, for each region, whichever of the cached and returned contours has the smaller error bound, and commits the whole merged set at once or not at all.

When a scale change brings the cached contours back within the display tolerance while finer contours are pending, the Workbench restores the cached highlight at once, without waiting or sending another request.
The Workbench retires pending contour work that a restored cache has made unnecessary and sends a best-effort cancellation for it.

When a partial refinement fails recoverably while its base cache and geometry are still current, the Workbench retries at once, only once, with a new request for the full original region set, reusing nothing from the failed attempt.
When that retry also fails, or the base cache or geometry is no longer current, the Workbench requests a complete contour regeneration instead of another partial refinement.

A partial refinement fails recoverably when its response is rejected for a missing, duplicated or invalid region result or for a precision miss, or when a transient interruption leaves a protocol-valid request without a verifiable response.
Protocol violations, malformed envelopes, unsupported capabilities and permanent runtime failures are never recoverable refinement failures and never use the refinement retry.

- Not imported: the performance budget and reference devices of Discussion #2 c36 decision 9 are acceptance targets whose tablet column awaits real-device measurement (#2 c39 Part B, issue #60), and the 24 CSS pixel cluster distance and Comments-tab copy are presentation. - Not imported as Rules or Clauses: the conformance-suite method of Part 4 (Discussion #4 c2 d1 and d3: an independent high-precision, interval or exact reference oracle, and adversarial affine families with rotation, reflection, high anisotropy, skew, their combinations and near-singular maps) is guidance for the conformance Scenarios (batch 8) and issue #25; the properties it checks are owned by {{C.preview-protocol.max-error}} and {{C.preview-protocol.amplification}}.
- The runtime's first report approximates rounded corners to an internal target of 0.5 iframe CSS pixels (code@6171f5d `src/preview/dom-geometry.ts#L85`); this is an implementation choice, since an initial acquisition declares no precision target (Discussion #2 c20 d1). Region IDs such as `r0` are opaque ({{C.preview-protocol.region-id}}).

features.summary: Non-recoverable Preview failures: the refinement failure latch and what clears it, the inline Preview diagnostic with its copy and technical details, and the manual Retry Preview action.

rules.statement: A non-recoverable failure of contour refinement ends that refinement and never starts a complete contour regeneration solely because of that failure.

After a non-recoverable refinement failure, while the cache misses the display tolerance, the Workbench keeps the highlight hidden and the Widget selected, and shows that precise highlighting is unavailable.

After a non-recoverable refinement failure, no new refinement starts within the same geometry revision until the geometry or context changes, a recovered runtime generation is confirmed or an explicit retry is taken.
Outer scale changes alone never clear the refinement failure latch or start a refinement.
While refinement is latched, cached contours that meet the display tolerance at the current scale are still drawn, and precise highlighting shows as unavailable again once they no longer do.

Runtime or capability recovery clears the latch only when a new runtime generation declares its capabilities again; elapsed time, reconnects, health checks, scale changes and further traffic of the same generation never do.

While the Preview session continues but geometry or refinement is unavailable after a non-recoverable failure, the Workbench shows a persistent, non-modal inline diagnostic in the Preview or selection context until recovery, context replacement or session end.
The diagnostic takes its title from the failure category and its body from the recognized reason, describing the impact and the available recovery, both from canonical Workbench translations.
For a reason it does not recognize, the diagnostic uses its category's generic title and body and shows the raw reason only in its expandable technical details.

The diagnostic's primary message states the failure category and its current impact; the reason and the applicable correlation identities appear only in expandable technical details, and raw stack traces or exception dumps never appear.
Every failure eligible for manual recovery in the same Preview session offers one shared Retry Preview action, never a reason-specific label, and activating it is an explicit retry.
While the generation that Retry Preview authorized is still in its handshake, the action is disabled.
Superseded contour work that a cancellation fails to stop never produces a Preview or Checks diagnostic.

features.title: Comment pins
features.summary: Comment pins on the Workbench canvas: the optional persisted pin hint and how it is set, moved, cleared and kept out of other records, where pins are drawn, and when they are hidden.

rules.statement: A thread's pin hint is display data only: anchor resolution, validity, comparison, filtering and re-anchoring never read it.
A pin hint is never validated against the View, the Widget's existence or size, a Variant or a render context.
Creating a thread may set its pin hint.
A thread without a pin hint draws its pin at the default placement.
A re-anchor that supplies a pin hint sets the thread's hint to it.
A re-anchor that explicitly clears the pin hint leaves the thread without one.
A re-anchor that neither supplies nor clears a pin hint clears it when the anchored Widget changes.
A re-anchor that neither supplies nor clears a pin hint keeps it when only the Variant scope changes.
Re-anchoring a thread to the Workspace always clears its pin hint.
Moving or clearing a thread's pin within its Widget is a separate action that never changes the anchor, records no actor and appends no history event.
The Workbench writes a moved pin once, when the drag ends, never streaming intermediate positions.
Pin hints never enter lifecycle or re-anchor history, submissions, Evidence records, formal captures or Decision provenance.
Re-anchoring back to an earlier Widget never restores the hint the thread had there.
A hinted pin is drawn at the hint's point within the anchored Widget's current rendered rectangle, so it follows the Widget when it resizes or reflows, in every viewport.
Pin hints are physical coordinates, so a pin keeps its side in a right-to-left Locale.
A pin that cannot be drawn at its point is hidden, never clamped or moved elsewhere.
A thread whose pin is hidden stays listed and navigable.
A thread with an invalid anchor draws no pin anywhere, and its hint stays inert until the same Widget resolves again.
Pins are drawn only for threads whose Variant scope is empty or includes the current Variant.
Workspace threads have no pin and never appear on a View's canvas or in its Comments list.
Dismissed threads never draw pins, even when the canvas shows resolved threads.
A comment's click point is transient: it only positions the composer, and the server never receives it except as a derived pin hint.

features.title: Prototype playback
features.summary: The Workbench Prototype player: playing a UX Flow from its entry step with a fresh View Runtime per step entry, following reported Widget Events or Workbench-driven advances, and what playback never observes or keeps.

rules.statement: The Prototype player starts at the Flow's entry step.
The Prototype player follows the same canonical Flow the editor edits; UIUX keeps no second prototype model.

Every step entry, including a return to the same step, a self-loop or a restart, creates a fresh View Runtime from the View IR, plugin defaults and the step's Variant, and leaving the step disposes it.
Interactive state may change within a step but never carries across a step boundary.
The Workbench player resolves each reported Widget Event against the Flow.
The Preview never receives the Flow and never reports a step.
Widget Events are observed only while a player has armed the Preview, so nothing is observed on the ordinary View canvas.
The player arms the Preview with exactly the current step's outgoing triggers, never a Widget Event that no transition references.
Each step entry accepts at most one transition from any source; a later occurrence, double click or racing advance for that entry is discarded.
The player learns only which armed Widget Event occurred, never its arguments or the input that caused it.
Playback history stays in the browser: it is never written to the Workspace, sent to the server, or included in Review, Evidence or Handoff.
The player always offers a labelled, keyboard-reachable Next control for each outgoing transition, even when the Preview reports Widget Events.
A Workbench-driven advance is a player action, not a Widget Event: it invokes no Widget Method, synthesizes no input and is never formal Evidence.
Commenting is allowed during Prototype playback.
Authoring a Flow keeps no log of Widget Events.
When the Preview cannot report Widget Events, the player works through its Next controls alone and says so.

contracts.title: Preview cross-iframe protocol
contracts.summary: The protocol between the Workbench and its Preview iframe: the wire channel and transport batches, the message envelope, field encoding and correlation context, Preview session and runtime generation identities and their gates, the capability handshake, the geometry stream, targeting and Widget Event messages, visible-region contours and contour work with their numeric conformance, and failure diagnostics.

clauses.statement: Protocol traffic travels by `postMessage` between the Workbench document and its Preview iframe as posts on the channel `uiux:preview:wire`: `{ channel, message }` with one envelope, or a batch `{ channel, messages }` with 1 to 256 envelopes and no other member. A receiver drops any other post on that channel whole.

A batch adds no identity, sequence, count or context of its own: the receiver passes each inner envelope, in order and independently, through the validation and gates of a single post, so an invalid envelope is rejected alone and a batch means exactly what the same envelopes sent as consecutive single posts mean.

Each side posts protocol traffic with its own origin as the target origin, never `*`, and accepts a post only when its origin equals its own and its source is the peer window: the current Preview iframe's window for the Workbench, the parent window for the Preview document.

Every protocol message is an envelope `{ type, context, payload }`: `type` is a non-empty, stable string from which the receiver selects the message schema, never inferred from the payload or a numeric code; `context` holds the shared correlation identities; `payload` holds all message-specific data, even when it is empty.

Required fields are always present, and an optional field that does not apply is omitted, never sent as `null` or another sentinel. A receiver ignores unknown fields of a known `type` while validating every known field; a field that a receiver must understand for correctness needs a capability or protocol-version gate.

The `context` key set is closed: `previewSessionId`, `runtimeGenerationId`, `viewId`, `variantId`, `runtimeContextVersion`, `navigationRequestId`, `widgetId` and `geometryRevision`, each present only when it applies to the message; `variantId` carries the Variant name and is omitted for the base state. Work-specific identities, such as contour-work sequences, snapshot versions, region IDs and interaction IDs, belong in `payload`.

`previewSessionId` is a non-empty opaque string that the Workbench generates fresh for each Preview session and gives the Preview document at bootstrap; the runtime only echoes it, and both sides compare it by equality, never by order.
`runtimeGenerationId` is a non-empty opaque string that the runtime generates fresh for each runtime generation; the Workbench never allocates it and compares it by equality, never by order.

A generation ID is retired for the rest of its Preview session once its generation ends, even if it was never acknowledged; a generation that reuses a retired ID is a non-recoverable protocol violation, and the Workbench rejects it and all its traffic.

Each side checks a received message's correlation outermost first: the Preview session, then the runtime generation, then the remaining identities the message carries. The first mismatch makes the message stale, and a stale message is discarded without effect: never staged for later, never adopted, never reactivating its generation and never by itself failing the current session or generation.

The handshake uses `capability.declare`, sent by the runtime with `payload` `{ protocolVersion, features }`, where `protocolVersion` is the protocol version the runtime implements, currently 1, and `capability.ack`, sent by the Workbench with `payload` `{}`. Their `context` carries only `previewSessionId` and `runtimeGenerationId`.

`features` is the generation's set of feature strings. Protocol version 1 defines `geometry`, `geometry.multi-target` and `widget.events`; adding an optional feature leaves `protocolVersion` unchanged, and the Workbench ignores a feature it does not know.

For each generation the runtime first sends `capability.declare`, echoing the session ID it was given. Until the runtime has received the matching `capability.ack` for that session and generation, neither side sends any other message type for that generation, and a receiver rejects any that arrive.

The first valid declaration of a generation pins its capability set before any acknowledgement. A later identical declaration in that generation is an idempotent duplicate that the Workbench answers with the same acknowledgement; a differing one makes the generation protocol-invalid, and the Workbench never acknowledges it.

A declaration without an acknowledgement keeps its generation, and the runtime may resend it unchanged; duplicate matching acknowledgements are idempotent and never acknowledged in turn. The protocol has no connection epoch, reconnect ID, handshake attempt ID, retry token or capability digest: the session and generation identify the handshake and its pinned capabilities.

A reloaded Preview document or a restarted runtime is a new generation with its own declaration and acknowledgement, and a retired generation is never revived. A pure transport reconnect keeps the session, the generation, its handshake state and in-flight requests, whose responses are accepted when they still pass the gates.

A new generation invalidates every geometry revision, region ID, contour-cache snapshot version and contour-work sequence of the previous generation; equal values in two generations never identify the same thing.

Widget geometry uses three messages: `geometry.acquire.request` and `geometry.release` from the Workbench, which carry no `geometryRevision`, and `geometry.acquire.response` from the runtime, which carries `context.geometryRevision`, the Widget's full rectangle `rect` and its `regions`. All three carry `navigationRequestId` and `widgetId`.

Geometry on the wire, including a commit's click point, is in unscaled CSS pixels of the iframe content viewport with (0, 0) at its top-left corner, after the Preview's own scrolling; it excludes the iframe element's border, its placement and every Workbench scale, zoom or transform.

`navigationRequestId` is the Workbench-minted identity of one geometry stream, whatever consumes it: a non-empty opaque string compared by equality only. The Workbench mints a fresh one for every stream it opens and never reuses one within a runtime generation, so a report for a released or superseded stream is recognizably stale.

`geometry.acquire.request` opens a stream for one Widget. A new request for a Widget with an open stream supersedes that stream at once, and streams for different Widgets coexist. `geometry.release` ends a stream one-way, unacknowledged and best-effort, and a lost release is no failure. Every stream also ends, without a release, when the runtime generation, View, Variant, runtime context or Preview session changes.

After its first report, a stream reports again only when the Widget's `rect` or `regions` change, each time with an advanced revision. The runtime coalesces changes to at most one report per stream per animation frame, never throttles below that, and sends no report and advances no revision while nothing changes.

Each `geometry.acquire.response` holds the full `rect` and the complete visible-region set of one Widget at one revision and is accepted or rejected as a whole: a missing, duplicated or malformed region rejects the entire report, and `rect` and `regions` never belong to different revisions.

`geometryRevision` is a JSON safe integer with its own increasing domain per Widget and runtime generation, never compared across Widgets. A true change of a Widget's geometry, including one caused by scrolling, advances it; the protocol has no scroll epoch or scroll-offset field.

Beyond the shared gates, a geometry report is accepted only when its `navigationRequestId` is the open stream of its `widgetId` and its revision exceeds the last one accepted for that Widget in the generation, which also covers the first report of a superseding stream. A report failing either check is stale for its own stream only.

A report with `regions: []` is a valid complete result meaning that the Widget has no reliably visible region in that revision, neither malformed nor a precision failure, and a later visibility change arrives as a new revision. A Widget without a rendered box keeps its stream open and is reported that way, with a `rect` of zero width and height whose `x` and `y` carry no meaning.

A runtime that declares the optional `geometry.multi-target` supports at least 64 concurrent streams and `geometry.release`; with it the Workbench opens at most 64 streams per runtime generation (`MAX_TRACKED_WIDGETS`), counting every consumer, and the runtime may silently ignore requests beyond that. Without it, the Workbench opens at most one stream and never sends `geometry.release`.

Targeting uses `targeting.enter` and `targeting.exit` from the Workbench and `targeting.hover`, `targeting.select` and `targeting.escape` from the runtime. `targeting.enter` names the interaction's purpose, `inspection` or `comment-range`; `targeting.select` names the committed Widget in `context.widgetId`, and `targeting.hover` names the candidate there when there is one. They never carry `navigationRequestId` or `geometryRevision` and need no capability feature.

`targetingInteractionId` is a fresh, non-empty opaque string that the Workbench mints whenever it enters or replaces an interaction, compared by equality only, with no order or persistence; a new one supersedes the previous one at once. Every runtime targeting message echoes it: one lacking session, generation or interaction identity is invalid, and one whose identities are not the active ones is stale.

Unlike other messages, a targeting message is closed: a member that its type does not define, in the envelope, `context` or `payload`, makes it invalid. A commit carries a click point only for `comment-range`, and the Workbench ignores one on an `inspection` commit. `targeting.hover` is sent only when the candidate changes, never for touch, and `targeting.escape` only during `comment-range`.

Widget Event reporting uses `widget.event.arm` from the Workbench, whose `context` carries no `widgetId` and whose trigger set holds at most 256 unique Widget and Event pairs (`MAX_ARMED_TRIGGERS`), an empty set disarming, and `widget.event.occurrence` from the runtime, whose `context` carries the Widget. An occurrence names only the arm and the Event: a runtime sends nothing else, such as Event arguments, input details or timestamps, while a receiver still ignores unknown additive members. Neither message carries `navigationRequestId` or `geometryRevision`.

An arm replaces the previous one entirely and is never acknowledged. The runtime applies it only when its View and Variant equal the runtime's render context, and a View or Variant change clears it. `armId` is fresh for every arm, never reused within a runtime generation and compared by equality only; after one occurrence an arm is spent, and the runtime reports nothing more until a new arm arrives.

A runtime that declares the optional `widget.events` observes only armed pairs, passively, so emission, listener order and the exceptions a plugin sees stay unchanged; it ignores armed pairs its Runtime lacks, reports nothing emitted before its Runtime finished mounting, keeps the arm across Runtime instance swaps, and reports an occurrence whatever caused it. A formal-capture Preview is never armed.

After the transport, session, generation and acknowledgement gates, the Workbench accepts an occurrence only when its generation declared `widget.events`, its View and Variant are current, it carries the current `armId`, no targeting interaction is active, its generation is bound to the open step entry, and its trigger is armed and resolves to exactly one transition. An occurrence failing any check is dropped without advancing the player and is never a protocol failure. Each Prototype step entry is one runtime generation.

Entering any targeting interaction first sends a disarm, an arm with no triggers and a fresh `armId`, then `targeting.enter`, on the same ordered channel, and replacing an interaction keeps the runtime disarmed. While a targeting interaction is active, the runtime reports no occurrence even when an arm is applied.

While the same step entry stays open, the Workbench sends a new arm with a fresh `armId` when the step's outgoing trigger set changes, when an exit leaves no targeting interaction active, and when it drops an occurrence that passed every other check but whose trigger is not armed or resolves to no single transition. A generation that replaces the step's generation during a targeting interaction is armed only after both its acknowledgement and the end of that interaction.

Contour work uses `contour.full.request`, `contour.partial.request` and `contour.cancel` from the Workbench and `contour.full.response` and `contour.partial.response` from the runtime. All five carry the `widgetId` and `geometryRevision` of the geometry they refine, and contour work never advances that revision.

`sequence` is a JSON safe integer in one domain shared by full and partial work per Widget and geometry revision, and a new geometry revision starts a new domain. The Workbench sends strictly increasing values that never wrap or repeat, and exhausting the range is a local invariant failure. Every contour request carries one, and its response echoes it exactly. After the shared gates only the response to the latest active request may commit: a newer request supersedes all older work, and a superseded or retired request never commits, even when its result would meet the current tolerance.

`snapshotVersion` identifies a committed complete contour cache. Only the Workbench allocates it, as a JSON safe integer that increases within the runtime generation and never wraps or repeats, and only when it atomically commits a new complete cache; requests, retries, staging and rejected or stale responses consume none. A runtime never sends or chooses one: a partial request names the committed version it refines as `baseSnapshotVersion`, and a full regeneration names none and is gated only by the shared gates and its `sequence`.

Each region carries its `regionId`, one closed outer `contour` holding its `commands`, and its `maxError`. A region set is an unordered collection identified by `regionId`: its order carries no z-order, index, priority or identity meaning, and a retransmission may reorder it. `contour.full.response` returns the complete set for the geometry revision and, like a geometry report, is accepted or rejected as a whole; a duplicate `regionId` is never merged or resolved by the last write.

`regionId` is a non-empty opaque string that the runtime allocates and the Workbench compares by equality only; it carries no order, index, coordinate or position meaning. It is unique and stable within one Widget and geometry revision, and a later revision may allocate new IDs. A full regeneration within the same revision returns the same IDs; when the runtime cannot keep regions corresponding, it establishes a new geometry revision instead of renaming them.

Each command is discriminated by `op`, one of `moveTo`, `lineTo`, `cubicBezierTo` and `close`, with absolute coordinates in the protocol coordinate space; an unknown `op` is invalid. A contour is exactly one leading `moveTo`, at least one `lineTo` or `cubicBezierTo`, and one final `close`, with no further subpath; `close` adds the straight segment back to the starting point, which the last point need not equal.

A region's contour, closing segment included, is a non-degenerate, non-self-intersecting outer boundary enclosing non-zero area; a runtime that cannot represent a visible piece that way sends no contour for it. A `lineTo` to the current point and a `cubicBezierTo` whose points all equal the current point are invalid; collinear segments and line-like cubics are valid. Winding, start point and direction carry no meaning, and command-array equality never identifies a region or cache. Receivers validate it before use and reject an invalid response whole, never repairing it by dropping commands, reordering, merging points or reinterpreting near-degenerate geometry; there is no geometric epsilon.

Every coordinate, control point, rectangle value and error bound on the geometry wire is a finite JSON number, and `-0` equals `0`. `maxError` is a conservative upper bound, in protocol coordinate-space CSS pixels, on the Euclidean distance between the region's true outer boundary and its contour, closing segment included, excluding stroke width, borders and antialiasing: at least 0, 0 only when proven exact, never underestimating, any overestimate valid. Every contour request carries `targetMaxError`, greater than 0, the bound it requests; a schema-valid response with any `maxError` above it is a precision miss, rejected whole and not a protocol violation.

A contour is precise enough to draw when its `maxError`, amplified by the current outer mapping into final Workbench display CSS pixels, is at most 0.5. The tolerance is measured after the actual outer transform, never in iframe or device pixels, and highlight stroke width, offset and antialiasing are outside it.

For an affine outer mapping the amplification is the largest singular value of its 2×2 linear part, computed by any method that never underestimates it; translation adds nothing. A non-affine mapping qualifies only with a proven bound over the whole contour and every point within `maxError` of it, never from sampled points; a mapping change voids that proof until it is proven again, and without one precision is unavailable. Such a proof needs no new capability unless it adds wire fields, changes error semantics or adds runtime obligations.

A partial request's `regionIds` is a non-empty set of distinct, non-empty region IDs of the base snapshot, in no meaningful order. A partial response echoes `baseSnapshotVersion` exactly and holds exactly one region for every requested ID and no other; anything missing, duplicated, malformed or without a valid bound rejects the whole response, which is never streamed, staged or partly credited. A response whose base is no longer the committed cache is rejected, never rebased, and the regions it omits are inherited from that exact base.

`contour.cancel` is a one-way, unacknowledged, best-effort advisory naming the exact `sequence` to stop under the shared correlation, with no reason or token; the runtime stops only matching active work, and only when it can. Newer work never waits for a cancellation, and there is no cleanup deadline. A lost, late or ineffective cancellation is never a failure, and the gates reject any response the canceled work still sends.

A non-recoverable Preview failure has exactly one category: `transport` when reliable communication cannot be kept, `protocol` for a message, correlation-identity or state-machine violation, `runtime` for a permanent Preview runtime or worker failure, and `capability` when the handshake, protocol version or a required feature cannot be satisfied. Finer distinctions go in the reason, never in new categories.

A reason is a stable, non-empty, lowercase dot-delimited code prefixed by its category, compared as an opaque identifier and never parsed for further state. The registry only grows: a code's meaning never changes and no code is reused, and a reason that must be understood for correctness needs a capability or protocol-version gate. A receiver that knows the category but not the reason keeps the category with its impact and retry semantics, and an unknown reason is never itself a protocol failure.

The initial registry is `transport.channel_unavailable` (terminal loss of communication), `runtime.unavailable` (permanent runtime or worker unavailability), `protocol.invalid_message`, `protocol.invalid_state`, `protocol.identity_reuse`, `protocol.capability_conflict`, `capability.unsupported_protocol_version` and `capability.missing_required_feature`. Transient interruptions, reconnects, reloads and recoverable generation changes use no terminal code, stale traffic that the gates discard uses no protocol code, and a malformed or conflicting capability declaration is a protocol failure.

A failure diagnostic carries its category, its reason, an optional detail and the correlation identities that apply to the failure's scope, drawn only from the shared context keys, `sequence` and `baseSnapshotVersion`, omitted when inapplicable and with no diagnostic-only trace ID. The detail is length-bounded, escaped or redacted for direct display, holds no credentials, Tokens, raw payloads, stack traces or exception dumps, and never drives control flow. A runtime never sends localized copy.
